why: Each new house at x fuses the run ending at x - 1 with the run starting at x + 1: that is union-find on adjacent points (merge, track component size). A lighter version stores each run's length at its two endpoints in a hash map, updating only those endpoints and a running maximum.
hints: When a house appears at x, only the runs ending at x - 1 and starting at x + 1 can change. What do you need to know about them?
Store, for each run, its length at both endpoints. The new run has length left + right + 1, and only its two new endpoints need updating.
Hash map point -> run length at endpoints (or a union-find with sizes); after each query update best = max(best, new length). O(1) per query, O(q) total.
pitfalls: Update the far endpoints (x - left and x + right), not only x itself.
The answer is the longest segment so far, which never decreases; do not recompute from scratch.
Coordinates can be negative or huge, so use a hash map, not an array.
statement:
Houses are built one by one on integer points of a number line. Initially there are no houses. queries[i] is the point where the i-th house is built. All points in queries are distinct, and a house is never built at a point whose left and right neighbours are both already occupied.

A segment is a maximal run of houses at consecutive integer points. After each house is built, record the length of the longest segment in the district. Return the array of these lengths, one per query.

Example: queries = [2, 1, 3]

  • Build at 2: houses {2}, segments [2], longest = 1.
  • Build at 1: houses {1, 2}, segment [1, 2], longest = 2.
  • Build at 3: houses {1, 2, 3}, segment [1, 2, 3], longest = 3.

Answer: [1, 2, 3].
constraints:
• Bounds are not stated in the source. Assume 1 <= queries.length <= 10^5 and -10^9 <= queries[i] <= 10^9.
  • All values in queries are distinct.
